cards.explanation: The answer is to go glean grain in the fields. This one is Ruth's idea. She tells Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, "Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor." Gleaning just means picking up grain behind the harvesters. Naomi doesn't hand her a plan, friends. Ruth walks in with her own.
The answer is False. Ruth the Moabitess asks to go glean, and Naomi replies, "Go ahead, my daughter…" That is a yes, friends, not a stay-home. Ruth heads out into the field.

The answer is Boaz. The text says Ruth "…happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech." Elimelech was Naomi's husband (Ruth 1:2-3), so Boaz is family. Ruth just happened to land in his part, friends.

The answer is False. Boaz doesn't walk up to Ruth first. He turns to the foreman of his harvesters and asks, "Whose young woman is this?" The question goes to the foreman, not to Ruth, friends. Then the foreman tells him who she is.

The answer is since morning with one short rest. The foreman says she "…has continued from morning until now, except that she rested a short time in the shelter." That is steady work with one short rest, bakers. Boaz hears all of it before he speaks to her.

The answer is field. Boaz says, "Do not go and glean in another field…" and he tells her to stay close to his servant girls. He keeps her right there in his own field, friends. Ruth gets a place to stay put.
The answer is True. Boaz tells Ruth, "Indeed, I have ordered the young men not to touch you." The order is already given before she even asks, bakers. I think that is a man looking out for her.

The answer is to drink from the jars the young men filled. Boaz says, "…when you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the young men have filled." Somebody else already did the hauling, friends. All Ruth has to do is walk over and drink.

The answer is why he would take notice of a foreigner. Ruth asks, "Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?" She is a Moabitess in Israel's field, bakers, and she asks it with her face to the ground. Her question is honest and humble.

The answer is mother-in-law. Boaz says he has been made fully aware of "…all you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband…" That mother-in-law is Naomi, friends. Word about Ruth had already reached him.

The answer is the God of Israel. Boaz says, "May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge." The wings belong to the LORD, bakers. Ruth came to a people she did not know, and Boaz says she took refuge with Him.
The answer is True. The text says Ruth "…ate and was satisfied and had some left over." A full belly plus a portion to spare, friends. I've never seen a better meal.

The answer is False. Boaz tells his young men, "Even if she gathers among the sheaves, do not insult her." It's an order, friends, and it's about how they speak to Ruth. She can gather there without being insulted.

The answer is to pull out stalks from the bundles for her. Boaz says, "Rather, pull out for her some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to gather." Then he adds, "Do not rebuke her." It's like a teammate leaving the ball right where you can reach it, bakers.
The answer is barley. After Ruth beats out what she gleaned, it comes to "…about an ephah of barley." An ephah is a measure for grain, friends. That's a solid day's work.

The answer is what she saved from her meal. Ruth "…brought out what she had saved from her meal and gave it to Naomi." That is the food left over from verse 14, where she "…ate and was satisfied and had some left over." She didn't come home with only grain, friends.

The answer is True. Naomi says, "Blessed be the man who noticed you." and only after that does Ruth tell her, "The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz…" Naomi blesses him first, bakers. She didn't even have his name yet.

The answer is that he is one of their kinsman-redeemers. Naomi says, "The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers." She says it right after Ruth tells her his name, friends. Family is the piece to hold onto.

The answer is until they finish gathering all his harvest. Ruth tells Naomi, "Stay with my young men until they have finished gathering all my harvest." The time is tied to the harvest being finished, friends. No week or day is named.

The answer is so nothing will happen to her in another field. Naomi says, "My daughter, it is good for you to work with his young women, so that nothing will happen to you in another field." It's Naomi's own reason, right in her words, bakers. Ruth stays put after that.

The answer is False. Ruth stays close to Boaz's servant girls "…until the barley and wheat harvests were finished." The passage names both the barley harvest and the wheat harvest, friends. She keeps at it through both.
